newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota seen marking record parent profit this year.
newsitem.headline: Toyota seen marking record parent profit this year.

text.p: Giant Japanese carmaker Toyota Motor Corp is expected to post its biggest ever parent current profit this business year due to the previous weakness of the yen and cost-cutting, industry analysts say.

Even though the dollar tumbled on Thursday to its lowest level against the yen since January, Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda said the current yen/dollar rate is not expected to affect exports by Japanese carmakers. He told reporters: "The current yen/dollar rate is not a problem."
The dollar fell to around 115.60 yen at one stage on Thursday, down nearly 10 percent from a 127.47 yen on May 1.

Car industry analysts expect Toyota's parent current profit to be between 730 billion yen ($6.29 billion) and 784 billion yen ($6.75 billion) in the current business year, ending next March 31, up from an estimated 620 billion yen ($5.34 billion) to 640 billion yen ($5.51 billion) the year before.
Toyota's record parent current profit was 733.80 billion yen ($6.32 billion) in the year ended June 30, 1990.
It will announce its earnings for 1996/97 and the outlook for 1997/98 next Wednesday.
"A weak yen and successful cost-cutting may bring Toyota's parent current profit in 1997/98 to 750 billion yen ($6.46 billion)," said Kankaku Research analyst Nobuaki Yanachi.
Analysts made projections for the current year assuming a yen/dollar rate of 120 yen, regarding the dollar's recent slip as temporary.
A rise in the dollar by one yen swells Toyota's annual profits by up to 17 billion yen ($146 million) by making its products more competitive in overseas markets, analysts said.

In November, Toyota forecast a parent current profit of 550 billion yen ($4.74 billion) in 1996/97, up from an actual 340.73 billion yen ($2.93 billion) the year before, and revised up its assumption of the average yen/dollar rate for 1996/97 to 107 yen from a May forecast of 100 yen.
"The impact of the weak yen is still very big for major carmakers, helping boost profits," Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura said.
The yen averaged 113.34 yen to the dollar in 1996/97 against 96.80 yen the year before, analysts said.

"Toyota will win (in domestic sales competition) this year with new models, raising its share of the domestic market by eroding shares of other makers such as Nissan and Mazda " Nikko Research senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima said.

Toyota's share stood at 39.2 percent in calendar 1996, down from 39.4 a year earlier. It slipped below a domestic share of 40 percent in 1995 for the first time in 14 years due to a delay in development of recreational vehicles. Okuda wants to regain a 40 percent share of the domestic market this year.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on non-operating activities such as investments in stocks.

Analysts expect its 1997/98 group net profit to be between 500 billion yen ($4.31 billion) and 590 billion yen ($5.08 billion) up from a profit of 430 billion yen ($3.70 billion) to 450 billion yen ($3.87 billion) a year earlier.
Toyota's record group net profit was 441.3 billion yen ($3.80 billion) marked in the year to June 1990. ($1=116 yen)
